subsection.title: Solids of revolution: disks and washers
subsection.p: A common way to make a solid is to rotate a plane region around an axis. The resulting solid is called a solid of revolution.
If a vertical slice rotates around the x-axis, it sweeps out a disk or a washer.

subsection.title: Non-circular cross sections
subsection.p: The slicing formula
does not require circular slices. Any cross-sectional shape is allowed, as long as we can express its area as a function of x.

exercise.title: Why is washer area \pi R^2-\pi r^2 rather than \pi(R-r)^2?

statement.p: A region with a hole after rotation has washers, not disks. In your own words, why do we subtract two disk areas, and why is the radius difference the wrong quantity to square?

hint.p: The hole is itself a disk. Area of a ring is outer disk minus inner disk. Squaring the thickness of the ring would describe a much smaller disk.

subsection.title: Choosing the slicing direction
subsection.p: The best slicing direction is the one that makes the cross-sectional area easy to write.
Sometimes x-slices are best. Sometimes y-slices are better.

exercise.title: How do you choose the slicing direction?

statement.p: Sometimes x-slices are best and sometimes y-slices are better. In your own words, why is the best direction the one that makes the cross-sectional area easy to write, even though the volume being measured has not changed?

hint.p: The notation \int A(x)\,dx or \int A(y)\,dy changes. The idea does not: add the area of one slice times its thickness.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: Disks and washers come from slices perpendicular to the axis of rotation. They are excellent when the cross sections are easy.
But some rotations make washers awkward. A vertical strip rotated around a vertical axis does not make a washer. It makes a thin cylindrical shell.
